pending_items.title: Hamas weighs response after Israel kills 10 people in Gaza
pending_items.content:
CAIRO, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Hamas chief Khalil Al-Hayya said on Thursday the group was not prepared to withstand continued Israeli attacks, after local medics said Israeli strikes killed at least 10 people in Gaza, including the Hamas-appointed deputy minister of education.

Hayya's statement was a rare sign of possible retaliation since Israel has stepped up attacks against the group in recent months, killing dozens of leaders and members.

In a third consecutive night of air attacks despite a one-year-oldceasefire, an Israeli airstrike hit an apartment in Deir Al-Balah, in the central Gaza Strip, killing Khaled Abu Nada, who was a member of Hamas'political office as well as deputy minister of education.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the attack was one of a series of targeted killings carried out recently against members and senior officials in Hamas, adding that Israel has killed about 80 Hamas militants in the past month.

"No terrorist is immune, and no one in the Hamas leadership will manage to evade us," Netanyahu said.

Abu Nada was the third senior Hamas official Israel has killed since Tuesday, after two senior security officials.

"The equation of killing and blockade cannot be accepted under the (ceasefire) agreement," said Hayya.

HAMAS SAYS IT WILL DISCUSS HOW TO RESPOND

Named Hamas' overall leader in July, Hayya narrowly escaped assassination himself ‌in a 2025 Israeli airstrike in Qatar that killed his son and aides.

He said his group would discuss with other Palestinian factions how to respond to "Israeli violations and the policy of daily killing," without elaborating.

The Israeli military said Abu Nada oversaw Hamas' economic portfolio and managed its banking and investment network, directing funds toward militant activities and force buildup. The military said his death may weaken the group's ability to sustain its finances and support its military capabilities.

Hamas confirmed the death of Abu Nada and that he was a member of its political office, but had no immediate comment on other allegations made by Israel.

It said Israel's targeting of academics and civilian figures was a "heinous crime".

Hamas said the continued policy of "assassination" violates the Gaza ceasefire agreement and international law. It holds US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace politically and morally responsible for failing to stop the attacks and for providing cover that encouraged further killings and attacks on civilians, Hamas said.

"Palestinian blood is precious and a policy of silence regarding the occupation's crimes is unacceptable from the Board of Peace and the guarantors," Hayya said.

Three other airstrikes killed seven people in the Tuffah neighbourhood, Beach refugee camp, and Sheikh Radwan overnight and on Thursday in Gaza City, medics added. The Israeli military did not immediately comment on those seven deaths.

Later on Thursday, medics said Israeli gunfire killed a 62-year-old man in the eastern Bureij refugee camp. The Israeli military said it was not aware of such an incident.

Israel has continued to carry out attacks it says target Hamas but the attacks have also killed many civilians. The broader ceasefire plan, backed by Trump, has not halted the violence or securedHamas' disarmament.

At least 1,600 Palestinians and 5 ​Israeli soldiers have been killed since the ceasefire was agreed in October 2025, according to respective Palestinian and Israeli tallies.

Israeli ​troops ⁠control around two-thirds of Gaza, up from more than half at the time of the ceasefire, while Hamas controlsa thin piece of territory along Gaza's coast.

Israel's assault on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since 2023, caused a ⁠hunger ​crisis, internally displaced Gaza's entire population and led to assessments of genocide ​from scholars and a United Nations inquiry.

Israel has denied the allegations of genocide, saying it acted in self-defence after Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took more than ​250 hostages in an attack on Israel in October 2023.

(Reporting by Nidal al-Mughrabi; Editing by Philippa Fletcher, Xevi Fontdegloria and Barbara Lewis)

pending_items.title: Netanyahu’s corruption trial: Is it really all over?
pending_items.content:
Benjamin Netanyahu got a boost on Wednesday , when judges in his long-running corruption trial recommended dropping the most serious case against him.

Netanyahu, who has been Israel’s caretaker prime minister since October’s election , is fighting to maintain political power as his rival Gadi Eisenkot tries to build a coalition.

He has also been fighting three corruption cases since 2020, when proceedings against him for bribery, fraud and breach of trust began.

In his telling, the trial has dogged his political career, prevented him from forming a government during a chaotic period of repeated elections between 2019 and 2022 and was responsible for “years of terrible suffering” for himself and his family during the investigation and trial.

Much of the evidence against Netanyahu rests on his efforts to secure favourable coverage for himself and his wife, Sara, in the national media.

The first, Case 1000, relates to accusations that he and his wife received gifts and payments in return for political favours. The second, Case 2000, concerns accusations that he struck a deal with Israeli daily Yedioth Ahronoth, whereby he would legislate to limit the commercial activities of their rival Israel Hayom in return for favourable coverage. Another, Case 4000, relates to accusations that he granted favours to telecommunications company Bezeq in return for positive coverage for himself and his wife on a news site owned by the telecoms company’s chair.

Judges, who do not have the power to drop charges themselves, have recommended that the Attorney General and Netanyahu critic Gali Baharav-Miara drop Case 4000, saying the prospects of securing a conviction were low, particularly over the bribery allegations. They also expressed doubts about whether the conduct alleged in Case 2000 constituted a criminal offence – and called for the matter to be reconsidered.

In relation to Case 1000, the judges suggested that prosecutors and the defence seek an agreement to bring the proceedings to a conclusion, although a verdict remained another option.

“The judges’ intervention is unprecedented in its nature,” said Barak Medina, legal scholar at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem. “They expressed their views before the prosecution had an opportunity to present its arguments.”

So, is this the end of the matter? Will Netanyahu continue to carry the taint of alleged criminality, and how might his career be affected?

It looks likely, but it is still too early to tell.

Responding to the judges’ suggestions, she said, “Every statement and proposal raised just now by the court” will be considered.

“We are open to examining everything. Including things that were argued in the past,” she said.

At the end of her remarks, the attorney general turned to the proposal by Netanyahu’s lawyers that proceedings be concluded through some kind of deal.

“We did this and were ready to accept his proposal, and we responded positively. Our extended hand remains.”

Baharav-Miara and Netanyahu are longstanding political opponents.

Baharav-Miara was among the staunchest critics of Netanyahu’s attempts to overhaul the judiciary and unshackle his government from judicial oversight in the early months of 2023.

She has subsequently challenged several government policies and decisions, including measures affecting the independence of the civil service, and attempts to dismiss the head of Israel’s internal Shin Bet security agency, Ronen Bar .

The Netanyahu-led coalition repeatedly accused her of obstructing its agenda and voted unanimously to dismiss her in August 2025, a decision later overturned by the Supreme Court.

In a defiant speech calling for the trial to end following the judges’ recommendations, Netanyahu said: “The boycotts must end, and now.”

He was referring to the refusal of opposition politicians to work with him due to his case.

“I know what enormous and immediate dangers the state of Israel faces,” he continued. “There is only one way to deal with them. To unite in order to deal with them. We must unite to secure the future of Israel – no less than that, and immediately.”

None of Israel’s main opposition politicians have yet commented on the judges’ advice.

Roi Zur, an Israeli academic at the University of Essex, said the main problem with allying with Netanyahu was not the corruption trial, but rather “ Netanyahu’s role in October 7 and the war that happened afterwards”.

“I don’t think a coalition with Netanyahu becomes more probable. [Naftali] Bennett, who was more open to such a coalition in the last two weeks, is still open to it, whilst the other three party leaders – Eisenkot, Lieberman and Golan – still seem to be against such a coalition,” he said.

Netanyahu has been accused of enacting government policies to derail his criminal proceedings. These include claims that he has prolonged the genocidal war on Gaza, putting his political survival ahead of Palestinian lives, a ceasefire and a deal to return Israeli captives.

The accusations intensified during his 2023 judicial overhaul, which opposition politicians, legal figures and protest movements argued would weaken judicial independence and provide Netanyahu with an escape route from prosecution.

In February 2023, former attorney general Avichai Mandelblit accused Netanyahu of pursuing the overhaul to bring his corruption trial to an improper end. Justice Minister Yariv Levin, the reforms’ architect, acknowledged that Netanyahu’s indictments had helped persuade the public of the need for judicial change.

The accusations extended to the conduct of the war on Gaza.

In May 2024, Defence Minister Yoav Gallant urged Netanyahu to put national priorities ahead of personal interests, criticising his lack of a post-war plan. A month later, Benny Gantz, then his principal political rival, accused him of obstructing a captive-release deal for political reasons.

In June 2024, former United States President Joe Biden said there was reason to believe Netanyahu was prolonging the war for political gain, a comment widely interpreted as referring to his corruption trial.

Most Israeli prime ministers to have served from 1996 to the present have at some point faced a corruption investigation.

In May 2014, former prime minister Ehud Olmert was convicted of bribery and breach of trust in several corruption cases relating to his time in office and as Jerusalem mayor. He served 16 months in prison.

His successor and Benjamin Netanyahu’s immediate predecessor Ehud Barak, a longstanding ally of disgraced American financier Jeffrey Epstein, was also investigated over allegations of bribery and illegal campaign financing in 2014 but was never charged.

In the late 1990s, Ariel Sharon was investigated over alleged payments to his son in return for political favours in a case known as “the Greek Island Affair” , but prosecutors dropped the case for lack of evidence.

In 2000, Ezer Weizman, who served as Israel’s president and previously as defence minister, was also investigated for corruption. While police said there was enough evidence to support a case of breach of trust and fraud, the statute of limitations had run out. Weizman resigned in July 2000.

pending_items.title: Saudi pop music is thriving — but for the right reasons?
pending_items.content:
Today, rapper Asayel Bishi is one of Saudi Arabia's rising hip-hop stars, signed to the country's biggest record label for new music, MDLBEAST. But not so long ago, she was making international headlines for a totally different reason.

In 2020, after Bishi released a music video for a song, "Bint Mecca," or "girl from Mecca," featuring people dancing in a local cafe, Mecca's governor called for the arrest of Bishi's whole production team. He said the video violated the holy city's local customs and traditions . In the end, the situation was resolved with a discussion about filming permits.

And by early 2023, Bishi was signed to MDLBEAST and has since racked up hundreds of thousands of streams on music platforms like Spotify .

In the past, other Saudi rappers have ended up in prison for similar, alleged transgressions. The fact that Bishi's story went a different way is probably partially because the 31-year-old's career path is on a similar trajectory to the Saudi pop music industry as a whole.

As part of Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030 plan , announced in 2016 and which aims to move the country away from economic dependence on oil, the country has poured billions into the local music industry.

The pace of development increased in 2019 after the country held its first major festival, Soundstorm, an annual event that now draws major international acts and over 400,000 guests. MDLBEAST was created then, primarily as the festival organizer. Since then, it has also become a record label, radio station, distributor, promoter and talent incubator.

A recent report for the Saudi Music Commission suggests the music sector could be worth $500 million (€455 million) by 2034. But it's difficult to figure out how well Saudi pop is really doing now because independent monitoring of the sector only began relatively recently.

Streaming platform Spotify reports that people listening to Saudi-made music inside Saudi Arabia increased by 195% between 2020 and 2024. However, the most-streamed artists inside the country are still international.

Although there was a mostly-hidden Saudi music scene before this recent boom, observers say the growth of the Saudi music sector is not organic.

It's all about building an industry from the top down, Amr Abdelrahim, a researcher at Sciences Po in Paris, reported in a 2024 study . "After 2016, young middle-class musicians and creative professionals, who had been careful to avoid drawing official attention to their countercultural activities suddenly became central to the ambitions of the state," he wrote.

The careers of young Saudi acts — like Bishi, for example — "became tied to the destiny of the crown prince," the researcher explained.

The Saudi royal family has long dispersed money from Saudi oil sales to their subjects, in order to ensure economic dependence and loyalty. But, Abdelrahim argued, "what is new about Saudi investments in culture under MBS is an unprecedented degree of centralization and the emergence of new clientelist networks around the country's de-facto ruler," using a common abbreviation for Crown Prince Mohammed.

Those involved "are inadvertently participating in the consolidation of the Saudi regime," he argued.

Observers say a lot of the new music businesses are vague about their ties to the state. But it's clear they couldn't work without the state's financial support and approval.

"Almost all major events are organized by the state or funded by closely linked entities," a spokesperson from Saudi-focused organization, ALQST for Human Rights, told DW. "This affects the type of music produced, as musicians have to be mindful of what is acceptable. This is not just about the music they produce, but also how they act and what they say to their fans."

ALQST believes Saudi musicians have even less artistic freedom under the new musical system than before, when they would have played or performed privately. They can lose their contracts and livelihoods, be prevented from performing or even arrested, ALQST's spokesperson said.

"In the past, the music scene was not regulated," explained the guitarist and bassist for Saudi black metal band, Al-Namrood. But now that it is, the state can more closely monitor musicians who once stayed hidden and only played privately, the musician, who goes by the name of Mephisto, told DW.

Al-Namrood are one of the rare examples of a Saudi act that isn't working with state support. The group first formed in 2008 but have never played at home and have kept their identities secret for almost two decades.

"The exchange is clear: You want to perform, it has to be under our rules," Mephisto continued. "And I totally understand the perspective [of some musicians]. But typically the artist must refrain from any criticism of the religious or authoritarian. [The state] doesn't necessarily buy an artist's loyalty, it just creates incentives that make criticism increasingly costly."

For Al-Namrood, who have often condemned Saudi conservatism, religion and politics in their music, that's not an option. "We don't want anything to do with them," Mephisto said.

In her 2020 paper for the journal, Arabian Humanities, Nora Derbal, a professor at the University of Hamburg, said Saudi artists told her that if they got a call from authorities asking them to participate in a government project, it would be an offer they couldn't turn down.

The artists she spoke with were debating "their cooptation and loss of autonomy, and about the consequences for not joining in state projects," she wrote.

On the other hand, in various interviews, Saudi acts who have partaken in their country's pop music renaissance have also been positive: They don't have to hide anymore, they can play for larger audiences and they are paid. In an interview, one Saudi DJ described the first Soundstorm festival as like "Berlin after the fall of the wall" while others said they felt they were making history.

"So that's the interesting paradox," said Fannie Agerschou-Madsen, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Roskilde in Denmark, who's written several papers on the topic. "We have all these social liberalizations and challenges to conservative norms but at the same time that's not being followed by political liberalization."

But that doesn't mean that some room isn't being created for meaningful change, Agerschou-Madsen told DW. Locals told her they enjoyed the newfound freedom of going to a dance party although, she noted, the subversiveness seemed to be more directed at the social conservatism than Saudi authorities.

Young Saudis are well aware of the red lines and state control of the music scene and are continually negotiating boundaries, the researcher argued. In that way, "their everyday practices create space for political and social change, little by little, although perhaps not in what you'd consider a typically revolutionary way."

So is the Saudi state co-opting local musicians, including those who might have said something controversial before they ever get a chance to?

A DW enquiry to MDLBEAST was not answered. And the answer likely lies somewhere in the middle.

For some young Saudis, the new music scene has been about fun, self-expression, belonging and creativity, Agerschou-Madsen wrote in a new, as-yet-unpublished paper shared with DW. "Others, however, view it as a top-down project that commodifies fun while sidestepping deeper issues of political freedom and social equity."
